content: A PARTICIPLE is a verb wearing adjective
endings. Latin reaches for one far more
often than English does.
It agrees with a noun in gender, number
and case, the way magnus does — while
keeping its verb's own meaning, and a
tense of its own.
mīles fortis     the brave soldier
mīles pugnāns    the fighting soldier
mīles victus     the beaten soldier
fortis says what the soldier is like.
pugnāns and victus say what he is doing,
or what was done to him.
Every participle belongs to a noun. Find
that noun and the phrase falls open.
Participles are built on the verb's own
stems, so a known verb shows a new face:
mittō → mittēns    sending
→ missus     (having been) sent
pugnō → pugnāns    fighting
→ pugnātus   (having been) fought
The endings are ordinary: -ns words bend
like ingēns, -us words like magnus.
Equitēs ā Caesare missī omnia loca
explōrant.
= The cavalry sent by Caesar
reconnoiter every place.
missī is nominative plural because
equitēs is. Nothing else in the sentence
could own it. Naming that noun is the
whole of the work.
Latin marks three participles where
English blurs two. Each has its own
ending and its own time.
PRESENT ACTIVE    -ns
pugnāns           fighting, as it goes
The noun is doing it.
PERFECT PASSIVE   -tus, -sus
victus            having been beaten
The noun had it done to it.
FUTURE ACTIVE     -ūrus
pugnātūrus        about to fight
futūrus           about to be, from sum
The middle one is the commonest by a long
way, and the only one of the three that
turns its noun into a receiver.
The time each carries is measured against
the main verb, not against today.
Mīlitēs pugnantēs cadunt.
= The soldiers fall as they fight.
Mīlitēs pugnantēs cadēbant.
= The soldiers fell as they fought.
Same participle, two eras. pugnāns runs
alongside the verb; victus closed before
it; pugnātūrus has yet to happen.
Expulsus errābat.
= Driven out, he was wandering.
expulsus closed before the wandering
began; errāns would have run alongside.
Some have hardened into nouns: īnstitūtum
is 'a thing set up' — a custom.
One participle, two jobs. Nothing in the
ending tells them apart; the sentence
around it does.
ATTRIBUTIVE is the plain one: the
participle describes its noun and stands
tight beside it, like any adjective.
Captam urbem mīlitēs dīripiunt.
= The soldiers plunder the captured
city.
Read captam urbem as one lump. Which
city? The captured one. The participle
picks the noun out; it is not a step in
the story.
English does exactly this much: 'the
captured city', 'the sent messenger'.
CIRCUMSTANTIAL is the working one. The
participle sets the circumstances of the
main verb: when, why or how it happened.
Multī mīlitēs aegritūdine cōnfectī
in castrīs manēbant.
= Many soldiers, worn out by sickness,
stayed in camp.
That phrase is a step in the story, not a
label on a noun. English wants a clause
for it: 'because they were worn out'.
Two signals sit on the page: the sense
asks for a 'when' or a 'why', and the
phrase often stands fenced off — many
editors print commas round it.
Which job is meant is a reading judgment,
not an ending to look up.
Every verb ending so far has named the
doer. A second set names the receiver.
ACTIVE          PASSIVE
spoliat         spoliātur
he strips       he is stripped
spoliant        spoliantur
they strip      they are stripped
The tell is an -r closing the word:
-or, -ris, -tur, -mur, -minī, -ntur
-tur and -ntur do most of the work in
real prose. Catch those two and the
others come easily.
Omnium animī ad laetitiam excitantur.
= Every heart is roused to joy.
The same -r rides on the past and future
of the present system:
spoliābātur    he was being stripped
spoliābantur   they were being stripped
spoliābitur    he will be stripped
Who did it? ā or ab with the ablative
names a person, a bare ablative a thing:
Hostēs ab equitibus spoliantur.
= The enemy are stripped by the cavalry.
Urbs incendiō dēlētur.
= The city is destroyed by fire.
Tier 7 adds the perfect passive — a
participle with sum — and takes up the
deponents, verbs that wear these endings
with an active sense.
